findings.statement: CXCR2 is the top convergence gene: up in UC biopsies (meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]), with a strong Open Targets genetic association [gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.8171]. Antagonists exist (reparixin phase 3, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682 phase 2, all in other indications); it is not loss-of-function constrained and has no curated safety events; no cis-pQTL or gut eQTL instrument, so MR is not tested (not evidence against); mouse colitis literature includes a CXCR2 antagonist ameliorating acute colitis.

CXCR1, the paired IL-8 receptor, is also up across cohorts and has Open Targets genetic support; it shares the same dual CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists (reparixin, ladarixin, navarixin, SX-682) so it is best treated together with CXCR2 as one neutrophil-chemokine axis.

CXCL8 (IL-8) is among the strongest expression changes and replicates in all cohorts, but has no Open Targets genetic association and plasma MR is null and does not replicate in FinnGen (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]). It is a good activity biomarker; its causal role is not supported by genetics (three instruments only; ABX-IL8 reached phase 2 in other indications).

CD274 (PD-L1) is up in UC mucosa, yet genetically higher plasma PD-L1 is protective (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]), colocalises with an IBD GWAS signal and replicates in FinnGen (OR [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; finngen_odds_ratio_per_sd=0.734]). The upregulation is probably a protective feedback; inhibiting PD-L1 (approved oncology antibodies such as atezolizumab) would be the wrong direction. Heterogeneity across the three instruments is nominal (p [gene=CD274; type=mr_sensitivity; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; layer=plasma_protein; heterogeneity_p=0.0259]); Steiger direction correct; not strongly constrained, no gut eQTL tested.

IL12B, an established UC drug target, has the strongest plasma MR in the whole screen: higher protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]), colocalises with the IBD GWAS and replicates in FinnGen and Liu 2023. This validates the MR design: genetics supports inhibition. It is the top Open Targets UC target.

IDO1 is strongly induced in all cohorts and has literature support (many mouse colitis papers, mixed direction), with inhibitors (epacadostat, linrodostat) from other indications, but genetics is absent: plasma MR null (p [gene=IDO1; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.111]), colon eQTL not significant and no replication. Inflammation-induced marker, not a genetically supported target.

CXCL5 is up in biopsies, but genetically higher plasma CXCL5 lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]); it replicates in FinnGen but does not colocalise with an IBD GWAS signal and uses a tag variant, so a neighbouring causal variant (the CXCL cluster) cannot be excluded. Expression-up and genetics-protective disagree; no drug.

FCGR2A has strong Open Targets genetic association and a modest but replicated expression increase, yet plasma MR is null (p [gene=FCGR2A; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.68]) with twelve instruments, and the gut single-cell eQTL (memory B) is also not significant; no drug. FCGR2B, not FCGR2A, is the strong plasma MR hit.

JAK2 is a known pathway target with high Open Targets association (score [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) and only a small expression change; approved JAK2 drug fedratinib is for myelofibrosis, not UC. No MR instrument (not tested). Genetically supported but barely changed in biopsies.

In gut eQTL MR the strongest genes are mostly not in the expression ranking; IRF8 in transverse colon raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IRF8; type=mendelian_randomization_gut; source=DATASET:MR_GUT_EQTL_UC; layer=colon_tissue; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.937]) and colocalises, with a single instrument. Gut-tissue genetics therefore highlights transcription-factor and epithelial-barrier loci (IRF5, GSDMB, INAVA) rather than the neutrophil chemokines, and blood and gut layers rarely test the same genes.

MMP1 (like MMP3, MMP7, MMP10) is strongly and consistently up with matrix-metalloprotease inhibitors (marimastat phase 3, doxycycline) from other indications, but Open Targets genetic association for UC is zero; useful as tissue-damage biomarkers, not genetically supported targets.

SLC26A3 is down in UC with Open Targets genetic support, whereas other strongly down epithelial genes (SLC26A2, HMGCS2, CLDN8) have no genetic association; loss of epithelial transport and barrier genes is consistent with consequence rather than cause except for SLC26A3. No drug.

caveats: MR uses cis-pQTL in plasma (UKB-PPP) and colon eQTL with mostly one instrument; many genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, JAK2) are not tested, which is not evidence against them.
Drugs listed are from Open Targets in any indication and are not UC evidence.
Mouse evidence is literature counts only (no MGI colitis phenotype for CXCR2, CD274, IDO1), direction not assessed.
Neutrophil-related genes may reflect immune infiltration rather than epithelial change.
JAK, IL23, TNF, integrin targets were identified from disease_top_targets only; MR was run for IL12B among them.
